title: Do Things that Don't Scale: recruit users manually and delight them
summary: Startups take off because founders push them, usually through unscalable work: recruiting users one at a time, over-delivering on experience, and starting in a narrow market. Big launches and partnerships rarely work. The unscalable effort also shapes company culture for the better.

principles.text: Startups rarely grow by themselves; founders must manually recruit the first users.
principles.quote: Actually startups take off because the founders make them take off.

principles.text: Measure progress by weekly growth rate; small absolute numbers compound into big ones.
principles.quote: The mistake they make is to underestimate the power of compound growth. We encourage every startup to measure their progress by weekly growth rate.

principles.text: Make the experience of being your user insanely great, even if the early product is buggy and incomplete.
principles.quote: It's not the product that should be insanely great, but the experience of being your user.

principles.text: Start with a deliberately narrow market to reach critical mass quickly, like a contained fire.
principles.quote: It's like keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs.

principles.text: Do manually what you plan to automate later; you'll know exactly what to build.
principles.quote: When you only have a small number of users, you can sometimes get away with doing by hand things that you plan to automate later.

principles.text: Big launches and partnerships usually don't work; happy early users matter more than launch size.
principles.quote: How well you're doing a few months later will depend more on how happy you made those users than how many there were of them.
